items.abstract: Dental microwear analysis is a widely used non-destructive method that provides insights into the adoption of specific diets, food preparation methods, and the conduction of paramasticatory activities using the mouth through the examination of dental features on the enamel surfaces. Recent methodological trends in the analysis of human dental wear have enriched the possibilities of the discipline, yet scarcely provide insights into the comparability of the values obtained from different microscopes on the same dental features. In this study, we microscopically observe the dental wear patterns of labial and buccal surfaces from 4 populations of the Iberian Late Prehistory, aiming to understand the level of intermicroscopy variability between the values of an optical microscope (ZEISS Axioscope A1 metallographic) and a 3D digital microscope (Hirox KH-8700). Within this framework, we adopt a dual microscopy approach, combining the existing methodological steps of the two microscopes, aiming to explore the level of agreement among the values obtained from both pieces of equipment. In this context, we provide, to our knowledge, the first ground for the quantification of diet-related wear patterns on human teeth using a Hirox KH-8700 3D digital microscope, underscoring its possibilities and observing discrepancies in the methodological implementation of the specific equipment in examining microscopic diet-related dental striations.

items.title: Understanding the intermicroscopy variability between Optical and 3D Digital microscopy in the quantification of human dental diet-related striations

items.abstract: Abstract The discovery of the Taung child, the holotype of Australopithecus africanus , marked a turning point in palaeoanthropology and stimulated the search for hominin fossils in Africa. Despite numerous Plio-Pleistocene hominin discoveries, particularly in eastern and southern Africa, Taung’s evolutionary position and relationship to other hominins remains unclear. Here we explore whether an eco-evolutionary range dynamics framework can help explain early hominin diversity in southern Africa. Focusing on the Taung child -the only unequivocal A. africanus specimen- we first reassess the site’s chronological age and examine the fossil’s dental and brain development, and M 1 dentino-enamel junction variation. These analyses confirm that A. africanus is a poorly defined taxon. Based on new palaeoclimatic and palaeoenvironmental evidence, combined with considerations about South Africa’s geographic position and the Zambezian–southern African biogeographic boundary, we propose that complex population dynamics, including drift and hybridisation, probably underpin hominin morphological diversity in southern Africa during the Plio-Pleistocene.

items.title: The Taung child and the biogeographic and palaeoclimatic drivers of southern African hominin diversity

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Traversodontids were diverse non‐mammaliaform cynodonts that occupied herbivorous and omnivorous niches during the Middle and Late Triassic. In Brazil, they are particularly well represented in the Santa Maria Supersequence, although the taxonomic status of some historically described taxa remains uncertain. Among them, “
                    <jats:italic>Traversodon</jats:italic>
                    (?)
                    <jats:italic>major”</jats:italic>
                    von Huene, 1936 was established on the basis of isolated cranial, mandibular, and postcranial remains from the Chiniquá region of southern Brazil. Here, we reassess the anatomy and taxonomic affinities of the specimens historically assigned to this species. A left maxilla (GPIT‐PV‐61005, here designated as lectotype) is the most informative specimen. It exhibits a combination of a broad maxillary platform, a maxillary recess, and strongly shouldered postcanine alveoli, supporting traversodontid affinities but not the original assignment to the genus
                    <jats:italic>Traversodon.</jats:italic>
                    These features are typical of deeply nested gomphodontosuchines, but do not form a unique combination of diagnostic characters that would allow a confident referral to any particular genus. The remaining specimens have no association or anatomical overlap with the lectotype and are here treated independently: the mandibular fragment is referred to Traversodontidae indet., the humerus to Eucynodontia indet., and the scapulocoracoid to an indeterminate non‐cynodont amniote. Accordingly, “
                    <jats:italic>Traversodon</jats:italic>
                    (?)
                    <jats:italic>major”</jats:italic>
                    is retained as a
                    <jats:italic>nomen dubium</jats:italic>
                    : its lectotype lacks autapomorphies, and the remaining specimens cannot be reliably referred to the same taxon.
                  </jats:p>
